sections.heading: On the Roof When the Adjuster Is.
body: After a big hailstorm, the door-knockers show up. Storm chasers sign you up, take whatever the insurance paperwork says, and replace only what the adjuster wrote down. If that's two slopes of a roof that took hail everywhere, you're left with the rest.
We work the other way. We meet your adjuster on your roof, so the claim covers what the storm actually did.
We get on the roof, or put a drone over it, and photograph what we find. Then we tell you plainly whether there's a claim worth filing.
If there is, Brady or Arturo meets your adjuster at the house and walks the roof with them. If the offer covers part of a roof that's damaged all over, we push back.
We can't tell you what your insurance company will pay, and nobody honest can. We can make sure they see everything that's on your roof.

sections.heading: What Hail Actually Does to a Shingle
body: Most hail damage can't be seen from the ground. Hail bruises a shingle: it knocks the protective granules loose and cracks the asphalt mat underneath.

The shingle still looks like a shingle. But the bare spot ages fast in the sun, and the crack opens up over the next few winters. That's how a roof that "looked fine" after the storm leaks two years later.

sections.heading: When Insurance Offers Part of a Roof, or Nothing
body: You get the letter and it covers a slope or two. The adjuster counted hail hits in a test area, decided some slopes didn't have enough, and called the rest "repairable."
But shingles don't repair like drywall. An older shingle goes brittle and cracks when you lift it, and a patched roof is a roof full of seams that the next storm finds.
Brady knows how this scope gets written and where it can be wrong. He checks the offer against what's on your roof, slope by slope, and pushes back where it falls short.

A denial doesn't always mean your roof is fine either. Sometimes the adjuster missed what was there, so we document the damage again and help you appeal. If your roof really is fine, we'll tell you that too.

sections.heading: What You're Seeing, and What It Usually Means
body: Most roof calls start with something a homeowner noticed from the yard or the hallway. Here's what usually causes each one, and what we do about it.

items.title: Shingles in the yard after high wind
items.text: Wind got under shingles whose seal strip had aged and tore them loose, and the ones beside them are easier to lift now. We replace what blew off, check the shingles around it and make sure the new ones seal down.

items.title: Dented gutters and granules piled at the downspouts
items.text: Hail hit hard enough to dent metal, so it almost certainly bruised the shingles too, even if the roof looks fine from the driveway. We inspect for free and photograph the hits so you can see them yourself.

items.title: Neighbors getting new roofs, and yours looks fine
items.text: Hail damage is easy to miss from the ground, and the same storm usually hits the whole block. A free inspection tells you whether yours took damage; if it didn't, we say so and you owe nothing.

items.title: A water stain on the ceiling
items.text: Water enters at one spot and runs along the decking before it drips, so the stain is rarely under the leak. We start at the stain and work up the roof to the flashing, pipe boot or valley that's letting it in.

items.title: A leak that came back after a repair
items.text: The first repair fixed something that wasn't the problem, often because flashing from the original roof was set wrong. We go back, look again and fix the cause instead of caulking over it.

items.title: Shingles curling or cracking on every slope
items.text: That's age and sun, and patching one spot won't stop the next. A full replacement is the honest fix, and we'll tell you if it's still a few years off.

sections.quote: They completed the repair that was thought to be the problem but still had leakage. They returned and did a thorough investigation of the area and found the original roofer didn't install the flashing correctly so they returned with material to fix that and we haven't had anymore leaks.
sections.name: Vicky S.

sections.heading: Roof Replacement
body: When the roof is done, it's done: hail-bruised across every slope, shingles curling, leaks you've stopped counting.

We tear off the old roof and look at the deck underneath. Then we put the new roof on, and plenty of ours go on in a single day. If your gutters took the same hail, we do the roof and gutters together, so you deal with one crew once.
When the job's finished, we sweep the yard with a magnetic tool so nails don't end up in your tires.

items.a: Yes. We get on the roof or put a drone over it, photograph what's there and walk you through it. If what you thought was damage is just normal wear, we'll tell you that and you owe nothing.

items.q: How can I tell if hail damaged my roof?
items.a: Look at the soft metal first: dents in gutters, downspouts, vents and flashing mean hail hit hard enough to bruise shingles. Granules piled at the bottom of your downspouts are another sign. Then have someone get on the roof, because the shingle damage itself rarely shows from the ground.

items.q: Do I have to file an insurance claim?
items.a: No. It's your policy and your decision. We'll show you what we found, and if the damage doesn't justify a claim, we'll say so.

items.q: Will insurance pay for a whole new roof?
items.a: It depends on your policy and on how much damage the adjuster agrees is there. You can check the offer yourself: the scope lists which slopes and how many squares it covers, so compare that to the slopes that took hail. If it's short, we document what's missing and push back.

items.q: What's my share of the cost?
items.a: Your deductible. Many policies set a separate hail and wind deductible, often a percentage of your home's insured value rather than a flat amount. Find that number on your declarations page before the adjuster visits.

items.q: How long do I have to file after a storm?
items.a: It depends on your policy, and the time limit is written in it, usually in the section on what to do after a loss. Don't wait to find out: hail damage is easiest to prove soon after the storm.

items.q: How long does a roof replacement take?
items.a: A lot of our roofs are done in a single day. A big or steep roof, or one with a lot of decking to replace, takes longer, and we tell you before we start.

If you decide to file, the claim has a rhythm: the inspection, the claim, the adjuster's visit, the scope of work, then the schedule. We're in each of those steps with you.
Replacing the roof is the easy part for us. The part that takes patience is getting everyone to agree on what's actually damaged.

Then we sit down with you and go through it slope by slope: what's damaged, whether it's a repair or a new roof, and whether there's a claim worth filing.

sections.heading: If the Claim Comes Back Partial or Denied
body: A partial offer usually means the adjuster treated some slopes as repairable. A denial can mean the damage wasn't shown clearly. Neither one is automatically the last word.

We compare the offer to the roof, document what's missing and push back with the insurer. We can't promise how an insurance company will answer, but we won't tell you to accept a short offer just to get a job.
Your policy, your deductible and your decision stay yours. We tell you what we see so that decision is an informed one.

body: A tear-off shows what the inspection can't. Once the old shingles are off, we look at the deck: soft or stained wood, gaps, old nail holes and flashing that was never right.
Bad decking gets replaced rather than covered. A new roof over a weak surface just hides a problem until it fails.

body: We work with all roofing systems and brands, so the recommendation comes from your house, not from what we happen to stock. We ask what you want from the roof, then tell you what we'd do.

items.title: Asphalt shingle

items.title: Wood shake

items.title: Metal

A tear-off sends thousands of old nails and shingle scraps off the edge of the roof, and some land in the grass where you'll never spot them. So before we leave, we run a magnetic sweeper over the yard and pick up the debris, and you don't find nails with your bare feet next summer.

items.q: How do I know my roof needs replacing and not just repairing?
items.a: Damage spread across several slopes, shingles that curl or crack, leaks in more than one spot and a roof that's had repair after repair all point toward replacement. Damage in one place usually doesn't.

items.q: Do you handle the insurance paperwork?
items.a: We help you document the damage, meet your adjuster and get invoices to the insurer on time. The claim is yours, and the final say belongs to you and your insurance company.

items.q: Can I replace the roof without a claim?
items.a: Yes. A claim is only one way a roof gets replaced. Call and we'll inspect it either way.

sections.heading: Shingles Blown Off in the Wind
body: You come home after a windy night and there are shingles in the yard, or you spot a bare patch from the street. A missing shingle exposes the layer underneath, and that layer was never meant to face the sun and rain.
Wind gets under the edge of a shingle whose seal has aged, and lifts it. Once one goes, its neighbors are easier to lift.
We replace what blew off, check the shingles around it and make sure the new ones seal down. That's usually a small job, and it's best done soon, while the damage is still small.

sections.heading: What Happens When You Call
body: A roof problem rarely waits for a good time, so it starts with a call back, not a week of phone tag. We set a time to come out and show up when we said we would.
We get on the roof, or put a drone over it, and look at more than the spot you pointed to. Older shingles go brittle, and the ones next to the damage often tell us how much life the roof has left.

Then we tell you what we found and what the repair will be before we do it. You get the repair and the reason, and if there's something bigger coming, you hear about it before it becomes an emergency.

sections.heading: A Leak Isn't Always Where the Stain Is
body: Water runs. It enters the roof in one place, travels along the decking or a rafter, and drips from a spot six feet away. That's why patching above the stain so often fails.
We start at the stain and work upward and outward until we find where the water gets in. These are the usual places.

items.title: A stain near the chimney or an outside wall
items.text: Usually flashing, the metal where the roof meets brick or siding, that was set wrong or has pulled loose. A bead of caulk covers it for a season; we reset or replace the flashing.

items.title: A drip below a bathroom or kitchen vent
items.text: The rubber boot around the vent pipe dries out in the sun and cracks. We replace the boot and the shingles around it.

items.title: A leak where two roof slopes meet
items.text: Valleys carry more water than any other part of the roof, and some were never sealed properly. We open the valley and seal it the way it should have been.

items.title: A wet spot around a skylight
items.text: Skylights leak at their flashing more often than through the glass. We check the flashing first and fix what we find.

sections.quote: After leaving a voicemail that the wind had blown off some shingles, I was called back the same day! We set a date and time for the estimate, and again he was punctual, clean, and professional. The repair was made as agreed upon.

sections.heading: When the Leak Comes Back
body: If a repair didn't stop the leak, it fixed something that wasn't the problem. It's frustrating, and it's common.

When that happens, we go back and look again, because the second look is where the real cause tends to show up. A roof that's been repaired by someone before can hide old mistakes, like flashing that was never set right.

sections.heading: Repair or Replace? We'll Tell You Honestly
body: Repair makes sense when the damage is in one place and the rest of the roof is sound. Replacement makes sense when the problem is everywhere: shingles curling across several slopes, granules piling up in the gutters, leaks in more than one spot, or hail damage on the whole roof.
If your roof is simply old and worn, we'll say that too. We'd rather tell you a repair will hold than sell you a roof you don't need.

sections.quote: They take the time to inspect, assist with the claims process if necessary, and insure the work is completed to perfection. They give you the information and allow you to make your decisions, it refreshing to not have pressure during the process.

sections.heading: Not Sure the Storm Did Any Damage?
body: If a storm hit and you're not sure whether there's damage, start with an inspection. We'll tell you if what you see is hail or normal wear. If it's a claim, Brady or Arturo can meet your adjuster at the house.

items.q: How soon should I fix missing shingles?
items.a: As soon as you reasonably can. Exposed underlayment can let water in, and the next wind or storm makes it worse.

items.q: Why is my ceiling stained but the roof looks fine?
items.a: Water often travels from the entry point before it shows. Flashing, vent boots and valleys are the first places we check.

items.q: Will a repair match my old shingles?
items.a: Close, usually, but not perfectly. Sun fades shingles, so new ones can look a shade different at first. If the old roof is discontinued or too brittle to work on, we'll tell you.
